nameStory: The pointed cingula gets its name from its distinctly sharp, pointed spire that tapers to a fine tip. 'Cingula' comes from the Latin word for 'belt' or 'girdle,' likely referring to the spiral bands that wrap around the shell like tiny belts.
description: The pointed cingula is a tiny sea snail that you'll need sharp eyes or a magnifying glass to appreciate fully. These delicate marine creatures belong to a group called micromollusks because of their miniature size, typically measuring just a few millimeters across. Their shells are cone-shaped with a pronounced pointed tip and smooth, glossy surface that can range from pale yellow to light brown.

idTips.label: Pointed spire
idTips.description: The shell tapers to a very sharp, needle-like point at the top - much more pronounced than other tiny snails you'll find on the shore

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Extremely small, usually under 5mm tall - about the size of a small peppercorn or grain of rice

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: Shell feels perfectly smooth to the touch with a glossy, almost polished appearance when wet

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Ranges from translucent white to pale yellow or light brown, often with a subtle shine

idTips.label: Spiral whorls
idTips.description: Shell shows distinct spiral bands winding around from bottom to top, like a tiny spiral staircase

habitat: Look for pointed cingulas in rocky intertidal zones along New England's coast, particularly in tide pools and among seaweed at low tide. They prefer areas with good water circulation and often cling to rocks, shells, or kelp fronds. You're most likely to spot them in the lower intertidal zone where they stay moist even during low tide.

seasonality.spring: Best time to search as winter storms expose new areas and the snails become active with warming waters. Look in freshly revealed tide pools.
seasonality.summer: Most active period with easiest observation during calm, low tide conditions. Check early morning or evening low tides for best viewing.
seasonality.fall: Still visible but may be less active as waters begin to cool. Storm-tossed specimens sometimes wash up on beaches.
seasonality.winter: Harder to find as they retreat to deeper waters or more protected crevices. Beach-combing after storms may reveal empty shells.

funFact: Despite being so tiny you could fit dozens on a dime, pointed cingulas are actually sophisticated grazers that use a ribbon-like tongue covered in hundreds of microscopic teeth to scrape algae off rocks - essentially giving each surface a thorough 'vacuum cleaning' as they move along.
confusionNotes: Other tiny shore snails like periwinkles are much larger and rounder, while pointed cingulas are distinctly cone-shaped with that signature sharp spire. Think 'ice cream cone' versus 'marble' - the pointed cingula always has that pronounced tip.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'micromollusk' refers to any mollusk under 5mm - a whole hidden world of tiny sea creatures that most beachgoers walk right past without noticing, yet they play crucial roles in keeping our rocky shores clean of algae.
compareHints: Since pointed cingula is the only Onoba species commonly found in New England, compare it to other small spire-shells in the Rissoidae family. Unlike its relatives, the pointed cingula has the most dramatically tapered spire and tends to be found higher in the intertidal zone than similar species.
